claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9112 §3: "request-line = method SP request-target SP HTTP-version". RFC 9110 §9.1: "The request method token is the primary source of request semantics; it indicates the purpose for which the client has made this request".

RFC 9110 §9.2.1: "This definition of safe methods does not prevent an implementation from including behavior that is potentially harmful, that is not entirely read-only, or that causes side effects while invoking a safe method." and "If the purpose of such a resource is to perform an unsafe action, then the resource owner MUST disable or disallow that action when it is accessed using a safe request method."

RFC 9110 §9.3.1: "The GET method requests transfer of a current selected representation for the target resource." §9.2.1: safe means "the client does not request, and does not expect, any state change on the origin server"; "the GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE methods are defined to be safe."

RFC 9110 §9.3.3: "The POST method requests that the target resource process the representation enclosed in the request according to the resource's own specific semantics. For example, POST is used for the following functions (among others):" - creating a new resource is one listed example among several (data-handling, appending). The RFC gives no frequency, so "commonly" (claim) / "usually" (lesson) is not supported as written.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation according to that resource's own semantics; creating a new resource is one example of such processing.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §9.3.4: "The PUT method requests that the state of the target resource be created or replaced with the state defined by the representation enclosed in the request message content."
RFC 9110 §14.5: "...or by using a different method that has been specifically defined for partial updates (for example, the PATCH method defined in [RFC5789])."
RFC 9110 §9.3.5: "The DELETE method requests that the origin server remove the association between the target resource and its current functionality."

RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "A request method is considered 'idempotent' if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request."

RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent." POST is not on that list; PATCH is defined outside RFC 9110 (§14.5 points to RFC 5789) and is not on it either. The item-adding PATCH is an illustration consistent with that.
RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "It knows that repeating the request will have the same intended effect, even if the original request succeeded, though the response might differ."

No permitted source states that browsers ask before re-sending a POST form on reload: HTML Standard / browser docs are not a docs root in content/versions.yaml and no browser was run. Nearest RFC text, §9.2.1: "A user agent SHOULD distinguish between safe and unsafe methods when presenting potential actions to a user, such that the user can be made aware of an unsafe action before it is requested." That supports the rationale, not the observed browser behaviour.
claim_verdicts.source: refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt §9.2.1, §9.2.2 (searched); no HTML Standard in refs/ or versions.yaml

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §9.3.1: "The response to a GET request is cacheable; a cache MAY use it to satisfy subsequent GET and HEAD requests unless otherwise indicated by the Cache-Control header field". §9.3.5: "Responses to the DELETE method are not cacheable."

RFC 9110 §9.2.2: "the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response"; "A client SHOULD NOT automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent"; "Some clients take a riskier approach ... a client might automatically retry a POST request".

RFC 9110 §15.3.2: "The 201 (Created) status code indicates that the request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created. The primary resource created by the request is identified by either a Location header field in the response or, if no Location header field is received, by the target URI." §9.3.3: server "SHOULD send a 201 (Created) response containing a Location header field".

RFC 9110 §15.3.5: "A 204 response is terminated by the end of the header section; it cannot contain content or trailers." §15.5.5: 404 "indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource". §9.3.4: "the origin server MUST send either a 200 (OK) or a 204 (No Content) response to indicate successful completion of the request."

Execution (curl 8.9.0, 2026-09-27): `curl -sv URL` sent "> GET /api/v1/orders/1 HTTP/1.1"; `curl -sv -d '{...}' URL` with no -X sent "> POST /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1"; `-D - -o /dev/null` printed status line and headers to stdout. `curl -h all`: "-X, --request <method> Specify request method to use", "-w, --write-out <format> Output FORMAT after completion", "-s Silent mode", "-S Show error even when -s is used".
claim_verdicts.source: reviewer run of curl 8.9.0; curl -h all

claim_verdicts.evidence: examples/don-hang@stage-0 Caddyfile: "There is no application behind these answers yet; that arrives at stage-1."; site ":8080 {"; order handlers use fixed `respond` bodies (@postOrder ... 201, @deleteOrder respond "" 204) and never read the body. docker-compose.yml: web service "shares this box's network so that localhost means the same thing in every lesson".

outputs/stage-0/scripts/http/methods.txt at stage-0 is identical to the lesson's output block: 200/201/200/200/204, "HTTP/1.1 201 Created", "Location: /api/v1/orders/13", then {"id":1,"customer_id":1,"status":"paid"} twice; consistent with the Caddyfile handlers. The live lab on this host runs a later stage (POST answers 401), so the captured stage-0 file is the evidence.

Opinion stated with its condition. Basis, RFC 9110 §9.2.1: "The purpose of distinguishing between safe and unsafe methods is to allow automated retrieval processes (spiders) and cache performance optimization (pre-fetching) to work without fear of causing harm", plus the §9.2.2 retry rules and §9.3.1/§9.3.5 cacheability.

issues.quote: a browser usually asks before re-sending it on reload
issues.text: Claim 11 remains unverified: browser reload behaviour has no permitted source (no HTML/browser key in versions.yaml). It is outline-mandated and hedged with "usually", so it does not block, but it rests on an unsourced observation where RFC 9110 gives a sourced rule.
issues.fix: Either keep the sentence and leave the open_question for the owner (add a browser docs key to versions.yaml), or tie it to RFC 9110: "the protocol asks a user agent to make the user aware of an unsafe action before it is requested, so a browser usually asks before re-sending it on reload", and add §9.2.1 to claim 11's source_hint.
